item.passage:
The gate at my aunt's nursery sticks in August, and she has never oiled it. I got there at seven, before the sprinklers, and shoved it open with my shoulder. I had come only to cover the shifts of the man who quit on her Friday. There was no wage in it, and no pane of mine to pay for. School had nothing to do with the day, and neither of us mentioned selling. A gravel path ran from the gate to the greenhouse door.

A card hung over the register on a loop of twine: NOTHING GREEN LEAVES HERE TO DIE. I had lettered it myself that morning, word for word as she dictated; the card was two hours old, she has never written one out in her life, she was not joking when she gave me the words, and she did not go against it once all day.

At nine a woman came in with a fig tree in a black pot, brown to the stem, and no receipt. She talked for a long while. Odile carried the brown fig into the greenhouse to nurse and told her to come back in autumn: no money out of the till, no second tree, no soil and no advice, and the woman went home with her hands empty. Nothing alive gets thrown out of this shop, she said. We had not grown that fig ourselves and it made no difference to her; a receipt has never decided anything here, and neither has a story from a stranger, and I am not teaching anybody a lesson.

I latched the gate at six. At breakfast I had told my mother exactly what my aunt would do, and I had been unkind and wrong about her. By evening the person I was ashamed of was myself. She had not been wrong about any of it, and I understood every step of what she had done. It was not admiration I felt, and there was nothing in the day to laugh at.
item.explanation: I had come only to cover the shifts of the man who quit on her Friday
item.correct_answer: a teenager filling in for a worker who has just quit

item.passage:
Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.
item.explanation: “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”
item.correct_answer: a launch sold off because her owner would not let a debt close the yard

item.passage:
Marta Sandoval spent thirty years compiling the first dictionary of the dialect of the high mountain province, working at a kitchen table between teaching posts. What happened to those finished pages is still argued about in the valleys she recorded. No volume of her own was ever bound, and she never paid a printer anything at all. The university library asked twice for the manuscript, and she had still not answered when the slips left for the capital; nothing reached the library. A newspaper offered to print one letter of the alphabet a month, and she refused to let the work appear in parts. A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name. A publisher across the border wanted a translation, but nothing of hers appeared abroad in any language.

One market day a week for nineteen years she stood among the stalls asking sellers what they called things, certain that people speak most truly while haggling over goods. She began each market day with the same question, the old name for a measure of oil, and set down whatever the first stall told her. A word went onto a card the first time a seller said it, without waiting for a second mouth. Parish books and wills she never opened, holding that a word owes nothing to having once been written down. The village teachers offered to have their classes write to her, and she refused: a child's page reaches the post already corrected. She kept no correspondents in other villages, saying that one market draws twelve villages to it, so postbags were waste.

Her name appears nowhere in his three volumes, not even among the thanks. It is no comedy, and hardly a waste, since the words did survive; her stubbornness is not the point, and impatience would be misplaced. The feeling the story leaves is indignation on her behalf, at a theft nobody has yet called one.
item.explanation: A compiler in the capital borrowed her slips for a summer, and eleven thousand of her entries stand in his national dictionary under his name.
item.correct_answer: a dictionary its compiler lost to a rival who credited her nowhere

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

item.passage: Novels issued in monthly parts end each instalment on suspended action, and critics now read the device as architecture: the break fell where the author wanted the reader held. The authors' own papers are less flattering. Revising for publication in volumes, when the monthly number no longer had to sell, the same writers ran parts together and smoothed the joins, so that a chapter that had ended on a fall from a horse now ended with the rider safely home. One of them asks his publisher whether "the usual precipice" might be spared from a quiet number and is told it may not, and the same letter discusses where a scene should end in quite different terms. For these writers the suspended ending was a matter of ______.
item.explanation: The writers dropped the breaks as soon as the monthly sale no longer required them, and one who asked to leave a break out was refused, so the suspended ending was something demanded of them: a matter of *obligation*. *design* is ruled out by "the same writers ran parts together and smoothed the joins": an author who removes the device the moment he is free of it did not build his book around it. *habit* is ruled out by "asks his publisher whether 'the usual precipice' might be spared"; a writer asking leave to omit the break is not producing it unthinkingly, and it was kept because he "is told it may not." *chance* is ruled out by the same request: a break called "the usual precipice" and negotiated in advance with a publisher does not fall where it happens to fall.

item.passage: Goalkeepers dive left or right on ninety-four percent of penalty kicks, though enough kicks are struck down the middle that standing still would save more of them. Economists call this action bias and put it down to the discomfort of doing nothing. Keepers themselves describe something narrower. Beaten after a dive, a keeper was outguessed by a good striker; beaten standing still, he failed to react. Both outcomes concede the same goal, and choosing between them is really a choice about ______.
item.explanation: The two ways of conceding are identical in the score and differ only in what is said afterward about the keeper, so the dive buys him a better account of the goal: the choice is about *blame*. *probability* is the rival the first sentence sets up, and it is the consideration the keepers are shown to be overriding rather than the one they act on. *habit* fits the ninety-four percent and is what the economists' bias amounts to, but the keepers' own explanation is a reason, not an ingrained reflex. *effort* is visible in the dive and would not distinguish the two outcomes, which cost the same goal either way.

item.passage: Seismometers everywhere record a continuous hum at periods of five to twenty seconds, produced when ocean waves press on the seafloor. Networks built to catch earthquakes filter it out before they look for anything else, since a small event is lost beneath it. Then researchers began to correlate the hum recorded at pairs of distant stations and found that its travel time between them measured the structure of the crust in between, as an earthquake would, but without the wait for one. On the earthquake networks the hum was, and remains, ______.
item.explanation: The second sentence describes how the earthquake networks treat the hum: they "filter it out before they look for anything else, since a small event is lost beneath it" — the standing of *noise*, and the blank asks what the hum was and remains on those networks. *an instrument* is ruled out by that same sentence, since a network that discards the hum before looking for anything is not using it to measure. *an anomaly* fails on the first sentence, "a continuous hum" recorded by "Seismometers everywhere": something constant and universal is not a departure from the norm. *a malfunction* is contradicted by "produced when ocean waves press on the seafloor" — the hum comes from the ocean, not from a fault in the instrument.

item.passage: The tolls charged on eighteenth-century English canals were fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act, which set both a ceiling and a floor: a company could charge no more than the published schedule, and could not carry one merchant's coal for less than it charged another for the same cargo. Historians have lately made the floor the traders' device, a guarantee that no rival would be given a better rate. The petitions tell it the other way. Those asking for the floors came from the companies, whose shareholders wanted an end to rate-cutting between rival canals. The traders' petitions do not mention the floor at all; they ask that the maxima be cut, and they complain of each revision of the act since, for a rate stood where the act had put it until Parliament moved it, and Parliament had moved it upward every time. What the traders feared was ______ tolls.
item.explanation: The traders asked for lower maxima and objected to every revision of the act, each of which had moved the schedule upward, so what they feared was the rate going up: *rising* tolls. *unequal* is the reading the second sentence attributes to historians and is ruled out by "Those asking for the floors came from the companies" and "The traders' petitions do not mention the floor at all": the rule against one merchant paying less than another was not the traders' concern. *hidden* is ruled out by "fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act" and "the published schedule"; the rates were public. *discretionary* is ruled out by "a rate stood where the act had put it until Parliament moved it": no company could alter a toll at its own discretion, so what the traders objected to was the direction of lawful change, not a company setting rates as it pleased.

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: On the other hand,
For instance,
In addition,
Therefore,
item.passage: Entomologists surveying moth populations often rely on light traps, which draw in species that fly toward ultraviolet sources. _____ many noctuids and geometrids ignore lamps entirely and are captured only by traps baited with fermenting sugar. Census totals depend heavily on which method a surveyor chooses.
item.explanation: The second sentence sets moths that ignore lamps against the species light traps attract, so the contrastive "On the other hand," fits. "In addition," and "For instance," would treat the sugar-trap moths as more of the same or as an illustration of lamp-drawn species, and "Therefore," wrongly makes them a consequence of ultraviolet attraction.

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: By comparison,
As a result,
After all,
Even so,
item.passage: Nineteenth-century ice houses along the Kennebec packed sawdust between blocks and walls; mill towns had it in surplus. Historian Ora Fenwick found that sawdust from resinous pine held moisture longer than hardwood dust and matted into a damp crust by August. _____ pine-packed houses lost roughly a fifth more ice over a season than those filled with maple shavings.
item.explanation: The damp, matted pine crust is the cause and the extra seasonal loss is its effect, the direction "As a result," marks. "After all," runs the other way, offering the loss figure as grounds for believing the preceding claim; "Even so," would deny that link, and "By comparison," would present the two facts as parallel measurements.

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: In other words,
For instance,
Otherwise,
Instead,
item.passage: Medieval masons cut personal marks into the blocks they dressed, and a recent census of these marks at Amiens has let historians trace individual workers across the building. _____ one chevron-and-bar mark appears in the south transept and again, forty years later, in the west towers. Historian Piet Vandal reads this as a long career, not a reused sign.
item.explanation: The chevron-and-bar mark is a single case illustrating the tracing the census permits, so "For instance," fits. "In other words," would restate the census claim rather than supply a case, and "Otherwise," and "Instead," both set up an alternative that the sentence does not offer.

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

item.prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Meanwhile,
Nevertheless,
In short,
Instead,
item.passage: Osier willow is cut in winter, when the rods are bare and the sap has drawn down into the roots. The fresh rods are bundled and stood in shallow water, where they stay until spring. _____ the basketmaker sorts last season's dried stock by length and thickness. By April both batches are ready for the bench.
item.explanation: The sorting happens over the same winter-to-spring stretch during which the fresh rods stand in water, so "Meanwhile," is needed. "Nevertheless," would mark a concession, "In short," a summary, and "Instead," a replacement, but the two activities simply run alongside each other.

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the recent model's claim?
choices: Subordinate birds on the periphery gain measurable warmth from the collective mass of the nest during cold desert nights.
Peripheral birds that attempt to move toward the central chambers are aggressively driven back by dominant pairs.
Central and peripheral chambers experience nearly identical rates of predation.
Colonies with more residents fledge more chicks overall than smaller colonies do.
item.passage: Sociable weaver birds of the Kalahari construct enormous communal nests, thatched masses that shelter dozens of breeding pairs for generations. Biologists long assumed these structures endure because cooperation benefits every resident more or less equally, each bird gaining warmth and safety from the collective. A recent model complicates that picture. It proposes that the colony is held together not by mutual benefit but by asymmetric coercion: dominant pairs monopolize the thermally stable central chambers and tolerate subordinates on the exposed periphery only because those peripheral birds absorb the brunt of predation and weather, effectively shielding the core. Cooperation, on this account, is a byproduct of exploitation rather than its foundation—an arrangement that looks communal from the outside but is sustained by the inability of the weak to claim the better rooms.
item.explanation: B directly evidences the 'asymmetric coercion' the model posits: subordinates are confined to worse positions by force. A supports the rival mutual-benefit view the model rejects. C would weaken the model by erasing the shielding advantage that motivates the coercion. D is true-but-irrelevant to whether the arrangement is coercive or mutually beneficial.
item.correct_answer: Peripheral birds that attempt to move toward the central chambers are aggressively driven back by dominant pairs.

distractor_rationales.choice: Subordinate birds gain measurable warmth from the collective mass of the nest during cold nights.
Central and peripheral chambers experience nearly identical rates of predation.
Colonies with more residents fledge more chicks overall than smaller colonies do.

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologist's hypothesis?
choices: Participants who actually delivered a lesson aloud remembered the material better than those who spent the same amount of time studying it silently on their own.
Participants reported enjoying study sessions more when they expected to teach the material than when they expected a test on it.
Participants told they would teach the material later recalled it better than those told they would be tested, even though neither group ever taught it.
Participants tested immediately after studying recalled more than those tested a week later, whatever they had been told to expect.
item.passage: A psychologist hypothesized that people remember information better when they expect to teach it to others than when they expect merely to be tested on it, because the prospect of teaching prompts deeper organization of the material. To isolate this effect, she wanted evidence that the difference arises from the expectation itself, not from actually explaining the material aloud.
item.explanation: Superior recall from the teaching expectation when no one actually taught isolates the expectation itself as the cause, exactly as the hypothesis requires.
item.correct_answer: Participants told they would teach the material later recalled it better than those told they would be tested, even though neither group ever taught it.

distractor_rationales.choice: Participants who actually taught the material aloud remembered it better than those who only studied it.
Participants preferred studying material they expected to teach over material they expected to be tested on.
Participants who were tested immediately remembered more than those tested a week later.

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument advanced in the text?
choices: In several countries, growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery.
A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.
Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies than countries dependent on a single export such as oil or minerals.
Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions of countries that were well governed before a discovery.
item.passage: The 'resource curse'—the observation that nations rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than resource-poor peers—is frequently taken to show that natural wealth is economically corrosive in itself. Some economists argue the correlation is misattributed. In their account, resource windfalls do not degrade otherwise sound institutions; rather, they tend to arrive in countries whose institutions were already weak, and merely make the consequences of that weakness more visible and better funded. Where accountable institutions predate a discovery, they find, windfalls are managed without any subsequent decline in growth. The curse, on this view, is not a property of the resource but a preexisting condition the resource exposes. What looks like wealth causing dysfunction is dysfunction determining how wealth is used.
item.explanation: The argument holds that weak institutions, not the resource, cause slow growth. Persistent slow growth after the resource is gone shows the dysfunction is independent of the windfall, supporting that thesis. The choice “growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery” restates the raw correlation the passage reinterprets and fits the naive 'resource is corrosive' view it rejects. The choice “Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies” is true but irrelevant to the causal claim. The choice “Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions” directly contradicts the argument's premise that windfalls 'do not degrade otherwise sound institutions,' so it would weaken, not strengthen.
item.correct_answer: A nation whose institutions were rated weak before an oil discovery continued to grow slowly even after the oil was depleted and the windfall had ended.

distractor_rationales.choice: In several countries, growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery.
Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies than countries dependent on a single export.
Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions of countries that were well governed before a discovery.

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize

item.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kowalski's explanation for the persistence of song complexity?
choices: Females consistently approached recordings of complex songs more quickly than recordings of simple songs.
Males with elaborate repertoires suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion than males with simple repertoires.
In a closely related warbler species, average song complexity has declined steadily over the past century.
Males raised in isolation developed markedly simpler songs than males exposed to adult tutors.
item.passage: The extravagant songs of many warblers are usually explained as honest signals: only vigorous males, the reasoning goes, can afford the metabolic expense of singing, so females who prefer elaborate songs secure superior mates. Kowalski's field data complicate this tidy account. Across nine seasons, males with the most complex repertoires sired offspring no more likely to survive than those of plain singers, and females paired with elaborate singers gained no measurable increase in reproductive success. Song complexity, Kowalski argues, is not being maintained by the benefits it confers on choosy females but by the simple absence of any penalty for producing it: once the trait arose, nothing selected against its elaboration. The distinction matters, because it reframes a supposed triumph of adaptive design as something closer to an evolutionary accident that natural selection has merely tolerated rather than actively favored.
item.explanation: Kowalski's explanation is that song complexity persists because nothing selects against it, not because it buys females anything. The finding that elaborate singers 'suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion' than plain singers is the direct test of that no-penalty mechanism, so it is the support. The finding that 'females consistently approached recordings of complex songs more quickly' is the tempting reversal: it is evidence for the honest-signal, female-choice account Kowalski's data undercut, so it supports the view he argues against. The report that in 'a closely related warbler species' complexity 'has declined steadily over the past century' concerns a different species and a decline, whereas Kowalski is explaining persistence in this one. And the fact that 'males raised in isolation developed markedly simpler songs' speaks to how song is learned, which is orthogonal to why elaboration is maintained once it exists.
item.correct_answer: Males with elaborate repertoires suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion than males with simple repertoires.

distractor_rationales.choice: Females consistently approached recordings of complex songs more quickly than recordings of simple songs.
In a closely related warbler species, average song complexity has declined steadily over the past century.
Males raised in isolation developed markedly simpler songs than males exposed to adult tutors.
